query: The (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy is a solid refrigeration working medium that exhibits a large caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field operation but has poor load-bearing integrity and tends to crack. What single intervention could increase its integrity while preserving caloric performance in these operating regimes? State one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its proposed mechanism, predicted integrity and caloric outcomes relative to the unchanged alloy, applicable field, pressure, temperature, and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with explicit results that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a thermomechanical treatment—specifically, cold rolling followed by rapid annealing to develop a nanostructured (fine-grained) microstructure—will increase the load‐bearing integrity and reduce cracking of the (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy while preserving its large caloric response under applied field and pressure-field operation.
generation.material_initial_state: (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 produced by conventional casting/sintering that exhibits a large reversible caloric effect but suffers from coarse grain structure leading to poor fracture toughness and crack formation.
generation.intervention: Subject the alloy to cold working (rolling) followed by a rapid annealing treatment optimized to refine the grain size into the nanometer regime.
generation.conditions: Thermomechanical processing conducted at temperatures below those that would induce deleterious phase segregation (e.g., annealing briefly at a temperature high enough to allow recrystallization but low enough to preserve phase composition). The caloric performance is assessed under the operational boundaries (applied magnetic field and/or hydrostatic pressure) and temperatures where the caloric effect is active.
generation.structural_mediator: A refined grain structure with increased density of grain boundaries that impedes crack propagation but whose interface characteristics remain sufficiently intact to allow the reversible phase transformation (martensitic or magnetostructural) underpinning the caloric response.
generation.mechanism: Grain refinement via cold rolling and rapid annealing is expected to produce Hall–Petch strengthening. The increased grain boundary density enhances toughness and load-bearing capacity by blunting crack tips, while the overall compositional uniformity and phase distribution are maintained so that the intrinsic caloric phase transitions are not adversely shifted or diminished.
generation.predicted_outcome: The processed alloy will exhibit significantly enhanced mechanical integrity with fewer and smaller cracks (increased fracture toughness and bending strength) while showing caloric performance (entropy change, temperature shifts under applied field/pressure) that is comparable to the as-cast alloy.
generation.baseline: The as-cast or conventionally processed (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy, which shows a high caloric effect but poor mechanical toughness with susceptibility to cracking.
generation.boundary: The beneficial outcome is expected if the processing creates a nanostructured grain size without triggering unwanted phase segregation or altering the reversible transformation responsible for the caloric response; if the annealing is too aggressive or the cold work too severe, the desired phase balance might be lost.
generation.uncertainty: The exact processing window (optimal degree of cold work and precise annealing temperature/time) required to achieve the best trade-off between improved integrity and preserved caloric performance is not yet determined and will need systematic optimization.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy samples: one processed by conventional methods (control) and one subjected to the proposed cold rolling and rapid annealing procedure. Characterize both sets with electron backscatter diffraction (to quantify grain size), perform fracture toughness tests (e.g., bending tests or crack propagation measurements), and assess the caloric performance under the same applied magnetic and pressure fields using calorimetry and temperature-change measurements.
measurements: Grain size distribution via electron backscatter diffraction or TEM.
Fracture toughness and bending strength tests.
Measurement of the caloric effect (entropy change, transition temperature shifts) under applied field and pressure-field cycling.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the nanostructured samples do not show a statistically significant improvement (e.g., >20% increase) in mechanical integrity (fracture toughness or bending strength) relative to the control without any deterioration (beyond experimental uncertainty) in the caloric response—such as a significant shift or reduction in the observed caloric effect—then the hypothesis is falsified.
